scenes.heading: Metallic bonding
scenes.sub: Why metals conduct, shine and bend without breaking
scenes.say: Copper wires, aluminium cans, steel bridges and gold rings. Metals all conduct, shine and bend without breaking. One simple model explains all of it.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Housemates pool spare cash in one shared kitty
scenes.science: Metal atoms pool valence electrons in a shared sea
scenes.breaks: electrons aren't spent, and the glue is electrostatic attraction between cations and electrons, not sharing.
scenes.say: Imagine a share house where everyone puts spare cash into one shared kitty. Metal atoms put their outer electrons into a shared sea, leaving positive ions behind. That sea holds the metal together, and because it moves freely, metals conduct electricity.

scenes.heading: The electron-sea model
points: A lattice of positive metal cations
scenes.say: In the electron-sea model, a metal is a lattice of positive cations in a sea of delocalised electrons. Metallic bonding is the attraction between the cations and that sea. It's non-directional, so each cation is pulled in every direction, not towards one neighbour.

scenes.heading: Why metals bend but salt shatters
scenes.say: Hit a metal and its layers of cations slide over each other. The electron sea flows with them, so the bonding holds and the metal bends. In an ionic solid like salt, sliding lines up like charges, which repel, and the crystal cracks.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Explain why copper is used for electrical wiring.
lines: Layers of Cu²⁺ ions slide over each other
Electron sea moves too: wire doesn't snap
scenes.say: Why is copper used for wiring? It needs to conduct and be drawn into wire. Its delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge. When it's stretched, layers of copper ions slide, the electron sea moves with them, and the wire doesn't snap.

scenes.heading: Reactivity series
points: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe
Easier to lose electrons = more reactive
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one
scenes.say: Metals react by losing electrons, so the easier a metal loses them, the more reactive it is. Potassium is near the top and gold is at the bottom. A more reactive metal pushes a less reactive one out of solution. Zinc in copper sulfate gets coated in copper.

scenes.heading: Changing metals
points: Brass: Cu + Zn; steel: Fe + small C atoms
Quenching: cool fast, harder but brittle
scenes.say: Alloys mix in different-sized atoms that act like speed bumps, stopping the layers sliding, so alloys are harder. For heat treatment, remember: slow and soft, quick and brittle. Annealing cools slowly and softens. Quenching cools fast: harder, but brittle.

points: Cations in a sea of delocalised electrons
Alloys are harder: layers can't slide
scenes.say: Quick recap. A metal is cations in a sea of delocalised electrons. Free electrons explain conductivity and shine. Sliding layers make metals bendable. Alloys are harder because the layers can't slide. Now try the practice questions!
